target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove the scheduling barrier that keeps millions from voting.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs would still be scheduled to work and would have to choose between losing wages and voting; therefore the holiday does not reliably solve the schedule problem for the people most constrained by work.

target: AG2’s assumption that a holiday is ineffective because it would not include meaningful enforcement or guaranteed time off.
objection: The objection depends on assuming the policy would merely change the calendar and leave private-employer scheduling untouched; but a holiday can be designed with enforceable voting-time protections, such as required time to vote or protected leave, which would eliminate the inequity concern.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday directly removes work-schedule barriers for voters.
objection: Even if Election Day is a holiday, private employers are not required to provide paid leave, so many hourly workers would still be working and would still face the same lost-wages-versus-voting tradeoff; the holiday alone is therefore not a dependable fix for the scheduling barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday leaves low-income workers stuck with the same constraints as an ordinary workday.
objection: A holiday changes more than the legal label: schools close, childcare pressures ease, consumer demand often falls, and many employers reduce hours or close, so many workers who would otherwise be scheduled can actually obtain usable non-working time to vote; the objection overstates how unchanged scheduling remains under a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday will convert into real non-working time for constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to close or give paid time off, so many service and retail workplaces can still stay open and schedule hourly employees; as a result, the “extra day” may not become actual voting time for low-income workers.

target: AG2’s assumption that low-income hourly workers will still lack usable time even on a holiday.
objection: The argument assumes too much continuity in scheduling, but a national holiday alters the demand and logistics environment: schools and childcare close, consumer activity drops, and many employers respond with closures or shorter shifts, increasing the amount of off-duty time available to workers.

target: AG1’s idea that a holiday meaningfully shifts voting off the ordinary school/work calendar for constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so the workers most affected by schedule constraints may still be working; the policy’s effect is therefore uneven and may mainly help workers with more flexibility rather than those with the least schedule control.

target: AG2’s claim that private scheduling remains mostly unchanged and that low-income workers are still stuck.
objection: That claim assumes private scheduling stays basically the same, but a national holiday changes baseline operating conditions enough that many employers either close, shorten hours, or schedule fewer workers; thus many hourly workers are more likely to have usable non-working time than the objection suggests.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday reliably moves voting off the school/work calendar for constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave, so workplaces can still remain open and schedule shifts; that means the holiday does not reliably create real non-working time for the workers most constrained by jobs.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a holiday is a broadly effective turnout strategy.
objection: As a standalone reform, an election-day holiday is not an especially effective turnout booster compared with reforms that directly change voting mechanics, such as automatic voter registration or enforceable time-off-for-voting rules; research-based expectations suggest its average turnout impact is limited.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a weak or symbolic turnout nudge.
objection: The objection understates the mechanism: because elections on ordinary work/school days compress available time and can force people to miss work or lose wages, a national holiday directly changes those conditions and expands non-working time to vote, which can meaningfully raise turnout.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday changes default conditions enough to give constrained workers usable time off.
objection: The key weak assumption is that low-income workers will actually get the day off or paid leave in practice; because private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off, many service workers will still be scheduled, so the policy does not reliably create non-working time for them.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday is just a mild nudge with limited turnout effect.
objection: A holiday is more than a nudge because it directly targets one of the main turnout blockers—conflicts with school and work schedules—by changing the default conditions under which voting occurs and expanding the pool of people who can vote without missing work or school.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday broadly raises turnout by giving constrained workers time off.
objection: That causal chain depends on low-income workers actually getting usable non-working time without wage loss, which a federal holiday does not guarantee because private employers can remain open and keep shift workers on schedule; the holiday may therefore help flexible workers more than hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only an indirect or weak turnout reform.
objection: The objection ignores that a holiday directly alters practical time constraints: when Election Day is a normal school/work day, voters have fewer usable hours and may have to sacrifice pay or responsibilities, whereas a holiday expands non-school/non-work time and removes that scheduling barrier.

target: AG1’s assumption that a federal holiday will shift school and workplace operating conditions enough to help low-income hourly workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so retail, food service, caregiving, and other shift-based jobs can remain open and keep employees on schedule; thus the holiday can widen turnout gaps rather than broadly eliminate the work-schedule barrier.

target: AG2’s idea that a holiday is just an indirect convenience measure.
objection: A holiday is not merely convenience because it changes the real-world schedule conditions that keep people from voting: it gives voters more non-school, non-work time to reach polls, wait in line, and complete voting steps without risking lost pay or needing special arrangements.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday will broadly reduce time-budget pressure for voters.
objection: The holiday does not reliably create usable non-work time for the people most constrained by schedules, because private employers are not required to close or provide paid leave and may still schedule essential hourly workers, leaving them with the same lost-wages-versus-voting choice.
